thread.title: When FAANGs Sink Their Teeth Into You - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Open Square Capital
title: When FAANGs Sink Their Teeth Into You - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Let's segue a bit from oil (yes, we write ALOT about that) and talk about something that's been in the news of late. Facebook. Along with Facebook, let's include the other companies that comprise the popular FAANG acronym, which stands for Facebook ( FB ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Netflix ( NFLX ), and Google ( GOOG ) ( GOOGL ).
Our fund continues to own Apple for many of the same reasons we mentioned in our earlier articles. We've owned Apple since the beginning of our fund and have a cost basis of approximately $120/share. In the 2.5 years since much has changed, but much as stayed the same. From a market perspective, the shares remain undervalued by about 20% if we benchmark against the "average" market multiple (i.e., at today's prices, Apple trades at 14x 2019 earnings (12x if we exclude the cash) as opposed to 18x 2019 earnings for the S&P 500). With tax reform having just passed, Apple recently announced that it plans to repurchase $100B of shares or about 10% of its market capitalization today and increase its dividend by 16% to an annualized $2.92/share (or about 1.5%). So from a valuation perspective, owning Apple isn't challenging.
We continue to believe that the shares are undervalued given the stability of the business and the inelasticity of the cell phone replacement cycle (i.e., consumers will continue to replace their handsets every few years). As the Apple ecosystem evolves, Apple Services will increasingly drive higher margins to Apple's bottom-line, supplanting an already high 30% margin handset/device business with a 70-80% service business. Increase profit, increase cash flows, rinse and repeat. That thesis is pretty obvious and akin somewhat to the razor and razorblades strategy; except in our case, there are 1.3B active razors comprised of $1,000 cell phones, $300 watches, and $500 iPads, and if the razor blades were spun out as a separate company, it would rank as a Fortune 100 company... by itself. Despite the doubters and the bears, Apple has continued to perform. As technology develops though, our Apple investment gives us a way to invest in something we see coming. Information.
Your New Reality Analysts and commentators have said FAANG stocks (i.e., Facebook, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) are overvalued that the market capitalization of these companies are too large and bound to collapse. Maybe and maybe the volatility of the market could drive down the share price. In fact, if the market turns down, it's likely many investors would sell these highly valued companies to raise cash, especially if client withdrawals are heavy, so assuredly these companies wouldn't be immune to the downdraft. As long-term holders of Apple though, we don't think such prices will be sustainable given the strength of these businesses.
More Than Meets the Eye The simple reason is that these companies aren't quite what they appear to be. As the companies have matured, the core businesses are becoming artifacts. Although they're the primary cash generating engines, Google is no longer just a search engine, Amazon isn't merely an online retailer, and Facebook isn't only a social media platform. Tech companies are transforming into data analytics firms, ones that have both the underlying data and the ability to examine and monetize that data. The breadth, depth, and constant evolution of that data will allow the FAANGs to dominate almost any other industry it chooses to enter. Already you see that with Amazon and its various forays beyond online retailing (e.g., healthcare, logistics, and cloud computing).
I Know What You Did Last Summer On a very basic level, these companies know almost everything about you. Your habits, preferences, finances, lifestyle, social networks, and possibly even medical condition. Take Netflix for example, based on your user ID, product registration data, your viewing patterns, and/or IP address, the company can easily deduce your sex, age, profession, and wealth indicators (i.e., income, marital status, household size, education, home ownership status, home value, and level of household debt). Cross reference that data with other publicly accessible data and the picture becomes even more complete. Depending on when, what, and how you watch certain programs, it can further determine what your general preferences are, when you're likely to be interrupted, eating and sleeping patterns, and health issues (do you pause your shows frequently for 3-minute breaks)?
That's only Netflix, what about Facebook? Uploading photos and "tagging" your friends or using Messenger or WhatsApp gives it a virtually unlimited source of personal information that can be cross-referenced to further understand who you are. Upload a picture with you standing next to the Eiffel Tower, Facebook's algorithms can automatically detect that you were in France, and the meta data in the picture gives them the time and date of your trip.
Moreover, when you upload photos, Facebook can scan the background and detect what you enjoy with your friends and based on other updates understand when, where, and with whom you enjoy it with. Similarly Google. Think about its open-source library of images called TensorFlow. If Google's machine learning algorithms are now sophisticated enough to understand whether you have onset glaucoma in your selfies, surely you have to assume they can deduce other information on your photos. A picture is literally worth a thousand data points.
Unsurprisingly, this data is evolving exponentially, and not just because consumers are willing to part with it but because of the internet-enabled devices or apps, we keep using. The devices or apps, with their bells, whistles, vibrations are just Pavlovian feedback mechanisms demanding physical action. It's constantly telling you to "upload/update your data," but in the guise of "keeping socially up to date" because doing so reaffirms your need for social standing/acceptance. Ultimately, these devices and platforms are designed to inculcate you to perform a specific, habitual, and recurring behavior, and that behavior continuously and in real time updates your profile for these tech firms for free. Thus, their very competitive advantage (i.e., their customer database), is evolving constantly for free. Actually not for free because you're paying for it.
Whether it's Apple Watches, Apple TVs, Amazon Alexa, Nest sensors, or Google Home matters little, these are all data gathering devices at their core, data which completes the consumer mosaic for our tech companies.
Someone's At the Door Here's an example. Amazon recently acquired a doorbell company called Ring for $1B. One billion dollars... for a "doorbell" company, but what if it isn't a doorbell? If you think about a doorbell, it could sit at the front of the house for years. Once you install the device, the game's afoot. Either based on the registration data or your IP address, Amazon knows where you live and your general household demographics (i.e., number of occupants, sex, marital status, general household income), and that's assuming you don't have an Amazon account already. If you do, then it completes another aspect of the data.
It's not just a security device, but an information gathering node for Amazon. It can track your daily patterns, who visits your house, what types of deliveries your house receives, when do you leave, when do you return, and the duration of your trips. If you shop using an Amazon credit card, it can understand where you go when you take those trips and what you bought. Cross-referenced with what you buy on Amazon, the company can then determine which deliveries weren't Amazon purchases, and based on credit card history, why that was (i.e., pricing, brand preference, etc.), and that's just a "doorbell."
Changing The Game In the decades to come, data and data analytics are game changers. They are the tools that will enable tech companies to ford almost any competitive moat. Today, tech companies have effectively created platforms to continuously collect and curate this invaluable IP. They have developed platforms that make the experience addictive, with reward systems in place to psychologically incentivize you to participate and contribute more. Currently, users give away their data because they assign little to no value in it. They think, who would want my pictures and who really cares what I did on Thursday night? Those token bits of data eventually coalesce into a pointillist portrait of who you are, what you do, what you like, and what makes you tick. Once these companies understand your preferences and proclivities, then everything is for sale, and just as its platform caters to immediate gratification, its businesses will eventually satisfy those needs.
Apple's Strategy So back to Apple. Now Apple has begun distinguishing itself from Facebook, arguing that "if you aren't paying for the product, then you are the product." Apple in the words of Tim Cook, its CEO:
We believe the customer should be in control of their own information. You might like these so-called free services, but we don't think they're worth having your email, your search history and now even your family photos data mined and sold off for god knows what advertising purpose. And we think some day, customers will see this for what it is.
Now notice that they're drawing a distinction between mining and selling the data. For most consumers, they'd recognize that it's one thing for a company to take the information and provide better services versus another to monetize and sell our information. The first is something we accept regularly, whereas the second raises privacy concerns.
As Apple navigates this evolving field, it's important to understand that its distinction does not prevent the company from monetizing its closed ecosystem. In fact, understanding this distinction may provide it with some structural and competitive advantages. Consumer trust in the Apple brand may benefit from this distinction, while still giving Apple freedom to operate and better tailor (and monetize) its products to you. More importantly, Apple's strategy provides a clear runway for Apple Services to continue growing without alienating its customer base. Today, Apple Services account for almost 1/3rd of Apple's revenues, and we anticipate this high margin side of the business to ramp further.
Given Apple's multiple, little of this is priced in, which is exactly why we continue to remain patient and well-rewarded shareholders. Among technology stocks, Apple is by far one of the cheapest ways to gain entry into this new reality. At 12x next year's earnings, we're effectively buying a leading technology company at a substantial discount to the market average and getting a "free" option on a data business.
So, honestly, we don't know if "this time is different." We don't know if FAANG is undervalued or overvalued given their businesses today and given their potential tomorrow. What we do know is this isn't your parents' GE, Xerox, IBM, etc. Something is different, and it's worth taking a breather to understand that before dismissing these companies on a valuation basis. Now if you'll excuse us... our watch just dinged and our tails are wagging.
